..
Issued at 1213 AM CDT Tue Sep 29 2026

A deep upper level trough over the Desert Southwest will merge
with the remnants of Hurricane Polo early this week and then 
move into southwest Kansas. Ahead of the system, widespread 
showers are expected today, with rain spreading from west to 
east. Some thunder could occur with the initial showers as some
potential instability will exist. Preciptable water values (up 
to 1.8") are forecast to increase to above the 99th percentile 
given the deep tropical moisture. 

Looking back through history, heavy rains from the remnants of
tropical systems are very rare across western Kansas. Atlantic-
Gulf systems tend to curve to the east of the high plains while
Pacific storms typically dry out over the mountains, with only
light to moderate rain occurring. In this particular case, the 
tropical system will get steered to the north and east and
accelerate due to the approaching upper level storm, leaving 
less time for weakening. Historical tropical systems that 
weakened and then dumped heavy rain across the high plains 
include the Galveston Hurricane of 1900 (4 to 6" from north of
Dodge City into eastern Nebraska and southern Minnesota) and 
the September hurricane of 1919 (8 to 14" across parts of 
western and northern Kansas), both of which were Atlantic/Gulf 
storms.

By tonight the remnants of Hurricane Polo will be absorbed into
the large upper trough and accelerate northeastward across the
southern Rockies into the southern high plains. The heaviest
rain will spread northward Tuesday night into Wednesday and end
from south to north Wednesday afternoon and night. Although the
various ensemble means indicate widespread 1 to 3" rains, with 
highest along and west of a line from Dodge City to Hays, there 
will likely be narrow corridors in areas of training that get a 
lot more. This is supported by the grand ensemble 75th and 90th 
percentiles for rain amounts over the period from Tuesday 
through Thursday of 3 and 4" respectively. Thus, the flood watch
was maintained for the Tuesday to Thursday time frame.
Additional periods of rain are likely Wednesday night and
Thursday as the upper low will be very slow to move away from
the high plains.

T-storms are expected to form Wednesday afternoon in the wake of
the heavy rain as the surface low and mid level dry intrusion 
arrive from the southwest. If modest insolation occurs and 
temperatures rise at least into the upper 70s, along with 70F 
dewpoints, then any convective inhibition would vanish, leading 
to isolated t-storms. Given the very warm temperatures at upper 
levels, which is characteristic of early autumn, lapse rates 
will not be supportive of very large hail; but marginally severe
hail and damaging winds can't be ruled out. However, given the 
increasing vertical wind shear ahead of the surface low, with 
with low level southeasterlies and moderate southwesterlies at 
mid levels, a few tornadoes can't be ruled out. The only 
significant tornado in western Kansas associated with the 
remnants of a tropical system occurred on 15 August 1880 in 
Dighton when 1 person was killed; but this was also an Atlantic-
Gulf storm. There is no record of this officially; but local 
office research uncovered the event.

The coolest air of the season will arrive Saturday morning as an
upper level trough traverses the northern tier of states and
pushes a cold front southward. Expect temperatures to fall into
the 40s across much of western Kansas by sunrise Saturday as
winds become light. This is only slightly below the
climatological average of 50. One limiting factor for 
temperatures is all the rain we will receive prior to the cool 
air arrival, resulting in higher dewpoints and less potential 
for radiational cooling. This will not be a very cold air mass 
by late September standards; but it will be a marked change from
the late summer heat.
